design_judgment.intended_result: All three candidates state a purpose, a required reader gain, and a material design choice that are mutually consistent and non-overlapping. Ledger 04 makes one canonical execution-fact authority with atomic batch families and explicitly refuses Execution decisions, Product Authorization policy, Data Governance custody, durable scheduling, and inspection presentation. Invocation 08 makes one provider-neutral bounded external computation per claimed Attempt that returns observations rather than committing them. Durability 07 makes one replaceable acknowledged-command surface that keeps canonical history in Ledger. The brief's declared decisions match the contract bodies; nothing in the slice claims implementation completion, admission, or provider selection.
design_judgment.authority_structure: Layer, canonical owner, parent, and owned system object are valid and distinct for each candidate: all three declare layer T2 under designDoc/agent_runtime_00_runtime_domain_contract.md, and their owned objects (execution facts and transaction semantics; invocation and model-visible Context; durable progress and recovery) do not collide with each other or with Registry 01 and Source Architecture 02. Decision ownership is generally well split: Execution supplies decisions and submits batches, Invocation and Durability return observations and receipts, Ledger validates and commits. Two authority defects remain. Invocation 08 section 3 assigns recording of the delivered Context and provider-native projections to Inspector, which the Runtime T0 defines as read-only and Ledger 04 itself lists as a derived surface. Invocation 08 also owns protected resources (Attempt workspace, authorized repository checkout, bounded shell, network egress, environment and credential injection) but publishes no ResourcePermissionManifest and names no enforcement point, deferring instead to 'external authority' — exactly the centralization the T1 root forbids and the pattern peer Registry 01 discharges explicitly.
design_judgment.boundary_coherence: Semantic owner, author, operator, reviewer, persistence owner, implementation binding, and admission authority stay distinct in most of the slice. Ledger 04 keeps record meaning with Ledger, Data Asset and custody registration with Data Governance, and migration and deployment admission with Software Delivery. Durability 07 keeps Temporal as a labeled replaceable Adapter and pushes tenant routing, Cell placement, and backend product selection to host composition. Ledger 04 correctly refuses cross-system atomicity and refuses to call an authorization service inside a database transaction. Two boundaries are not coherent. Invocation 08 blurs persistence owner and read-only projection in the Inspector sentence. Durability 07 places 'backend binding selected by the host' inside the frozen command in section 3 while section 8 routes backend binding and deployment-specific namespace, endpoint, queue, credentials, region, and placement through a secure Adapter configuration and declares those values non-Durability types; the same named value therefore has two channels and no rule separating them.
design_judgment.inheritance_and_dependencies: The target import direction is preserved at the responsibility level: Durability reconciles 'through Execution' rather than reading Ledger, Ledger records durable acknowledgements supplied 'by Durability through Execution', and Invocation resolves Adapter releases through Registry, which is an allowed edge. Inherited constraint closure is incomplete in three places. Ledger 04 states only that timestamp fields retain 'instant semantics and format', omitting the Timestamp Semantics rules that the authoritative store assigns recorded_at_utc at atomic commit and that every concrete persisted class carries an exact registration — both of which peer Registry 01 states for its own store. Invocation 08 omits designDoc/the_timestamp_semantic.md from inherits entirely although it is the sole entry point for provider-reported instants, protected-operation deadlines, timeouts, and workspace retention. Ledger 04 assigns itself execution of a fail-closed comparison 'supplied by document 09' without declaring the channel, while the T1 dependency graph gives Ledger no edge to the authority ports and Source Architecture bars the supporting foundation from satisfying a protected predicate.
design_judgment.intent_code_separation: Stable intent is well separated from mutable implementation truth. None of the three candidates carries a file inventory, current release pointer, test result, delivery status, or admission claim. Each change-boundary section defers exact fields, schemas, predecessor disposition, migration, and rollback to a later Code Design Basis after the complete contract set is accepted, and each states that missing real integration evidence remains validation debt rather than conformance. Technology names appear only as labeled replaceable bindings or negative examples (PostgreSQL connections and ORM sessions as things the ports must not expose; Temporal as one Adapter that the contract explicitly does not select as a product dependency). No mutable provider, path, or release fact is presented as Design Intent.
design_judgment.implementability: An implementer can form a Code Design Basis for most of this slice: the record families, atomic transaction families, port set, capability classes, structured-output modes, context-continuity modes, frozen command law, bounded snapshot, and intent-to-acknowledgement recovery pattern are concrete enough to build against without inventing product behavior. Three gaps would force redesign or invention. Ledger 04 does not say how the registered fence predicate, clock profile, and health evidence reach the transaction that must evaluate them, so an implementer must choose between a forbidden reverse import, a foundation implementation the architecture contract prohibits, or an invented parameter. Durability 07 declares no provider-neutral inbound boundary for backend-initiated progress — a fired timer, a satisfied wait, or worker dispatch re-entering Execution — mentioning it only inside the Temporal-specific mapping as 'a host-composed bridge'. Ledger 04's content port declares staging, hash verification, ref binding, and disposition but no authorized body-retrieval boundary or explicit body-unavailable result, which the later Inspection contract would otherwise have to invent.

findings.quoted_evidence: Inspector records the exact complete envelope and every provider-native projection separately. It does not display prompt fragments as if they were independent invocations.
findings.requirement: The Runtime T0 section 4 invariant 7 states that 'Inspection is read-only, receives authorization before retrieval, and exposes bounded projections rather than loading an unbounded history.' Ledger 04 section 1 states that 'Provider transcripts, CLI workspaces, Temporal history, Inspector projections, in-memory result objects, and usage aggregates are derived or operational surfaces. None is a second Ledger.' Design Doc Management section 6 requires the persistence owner and the operator or projection surface to remain distinguishable, and treats ambiguous prose as a design finding when it changes who may write.
findings.impact: The delivered model Context and its provider-native projections are the only evidence of what the model actually saw, and this sentence makes a read-only projection responsibility their recorder. It creates a second write path beside the canonical Ledger, contradicts Charter completion condition 4, and contradicts this same candidate's section 2, where the InvocationResult already returns 'delivered Context and provider-native output-constraint evidence refs' as observations for Execution to commit. An implementer could legitimately build envelope capture inside Inspection and leave no canonical record family for it.

findings.requirement: Timestamp Semantics section 5 assigns provider timestamps the status of 'Observational execution evidence only unless a typed domain projection admits them' and restricts the monotonic process clock to local durations and timeouts that 'never persist as a cross-process business timestamp'. Section 9 makes it non-conformant when 'a caller, worker, provider, or durable backend assigns another store's `recorded_at_utc`'. The Runtime T0 section 9 records Timestamp Semantics as an external authority whose exact authorities Runtime 'consumes and records'.
findings.impact: Invocation is the sole point at which provider-reported instants enter Runtime, and it also defines a protected-operation 'deadline', provider-turn and timeout budgets, and workspace retention. Omitting Timestamp Semantics from the inherited set leaves the contract with no rule that provider instants stay observational, that timeouts stay monotonic and local, or that Invocation observations never carry a Ledger commit instant. Peers Ledger 04 and Durability 07 both inherit the contract, and Durability even pins a 'Timestamp-governed deadline', so the omission is a closure gap in the peer set rather than an editorial one.

findings.quoted_evidence: Timestamp fields retain the instant semantics and format required by Timestamp Governance. They describe when an observation occurred. They do not establish transaction order or replay identity.
findings.requirement: Timestamp Semantics section 2 states that 'Every persisted record has `recorded_at_utc`' and that `recorded_at` is 'Assigned by that store, not by a caller, worker, or provider'. Section 4 states that 'Every concrete persisted class therefore requires its own exact registration' and that unregistered persisted classes fail validation. Section 9 makes it non-conformant when 'an unregistered class writes time-bearing records'.
findings.impact: Ledger 04 owns the largest persisted record family in the Runtime and receives time-bearing observations from Invocation, Durability, and External Authority Integration, but it states only the format and ordering half of the inherited law. It never states that the Ledger store assigns `recorded_at_utc` at atomic commit, nor that every concrete persisted Ledger class carries an exact Timestamp class registration. An implementer may therefore accept caller-supplied or provider-supplied commit instants inside a batch, which is precisely the non-conformance Timestamp Semantics section 9 names. Peer Registry 01 section 9 states both obligations for its own store, so the inherited constraint closes for Registry and not for Ledger.

findings.impact: Every operation in the section 2 port table is outbound. The contract never declares how backend-initiated progress — a fired retry or wait timer, a satisfied wait, or worker dispatch after replacement — re-enters Runtime Execution. The only statement of that path is Temporal-specific: 'Activities enter Runtime Execution through a host-composed bridge using stable refs.' A maintainer implementing a non-Temporal backend, which is the stated purpose of this contract, must invent the inbound contract, and its ownership between Durability, Execution 10, and host composition is unassigned. The section 11 adapter conformance list likewise proves no inbound behavior.
